supported: Position: on arriving near the cemetery Wiedrich was ordered to a hill on the north side of the Baltimore turnpike, near the cemetery and east of the town; Hunt places it on the hill in front of the cemetery entrance
In the afternoon the battery skirmished with a rebel battery posted near the road from Gettysburg to York

About 5 p.m., when the Union infantry that had advanced through the town was repulsed, he opened with shells on the columns advancing from the town, with good effect; canister then checked the enemy in front; fire kept up until late in the evening
About 4.30 p.m. the enemy's single attempt to turn the right, ascending the slope northeast of Gettysburg, was broken by Wiedrich's battery

Earlier, after about 2.45 p.m. (Howard: 'About this time (2.45 p. m.) the enemy showed himself in force in front of the Eleventh Corps'), a Confederate battery a little more than a mile north of the cemetery near the Harrisburg road could be seen and Howard directed Wiedrich's 3-inch battery to fire; the shells for the most part fell short
not_supported: The target 'Confederates at the railroad cut'

closeout.claim: Wiedrich's battery stood on a hill north of the Baltimore turnpike near the cemetery and east of the town (Hunt: in front of the cemetery entrance). During the afternoon it skirmished with a rebel battery posted near the York road. About 5 p.m., when the Union infantry that had advanced through the town was repulsed, Wiedrich changed the direction of his pieces, opened with shells on the columns advancing from the town, and then fired canister at the enemy that appeared in front; the fire was kept up until late in the evening. Howard and Hunt place the enemy's single attempt to turn the right at about 4.30 p.m. and say Wiedrich's battery broke the line. Nothing in the reports ties this fire to the railroad cut (the cut lies on Oak Ridge, far from his front).
remains_unsupported: Any target of Wiedrich's fire at 'the railroad cut' (not in any report); the source the seed cites is secondary and was not retrievable.

He later moved through the town and was assigned a position on Cemetery Hill on the left wing of the corps batteries

closeout.claim: Wheeler marched from Emmitsburg with Steinwehr's division, was ordered forward at double-quick when about 5 miles from Gettysburg, took position on the right of the town, then moved through the town to support Dilger's battery and fought on Dilger's right (two caisson bodies broke down in the town, one of them recovered; a piece was dismounted, abandoned and recovered on the 5th). He then moved back through the town and was assigned a position on Cemetery Hill, on the left wing of the corps batteries. On Jul 2 the battery threw a few shells at the rebel train in the morning and replied to the rebel batteries that opened at about 2 p.m.

closeout.claim: At 5.25 p.m. Hancock wrote from the cemetery: when he arrived 'an hour since' he found the troops had given up the front of Gettysburg and the town; the troops had taken a position in the cemetery that 'cannot well be taken' but is easily turned; Slocum was coming on the ground and taking position on the right; there were no troops on the left, the Third Corps not having reported; Gibbon had better march up to a commanding position on the right or left; the battle was quiet and he thought all would be right until night; trains had been sent back; 'I think we can retire; if not, we can fight here, as the ground appears not unfavorable with good troops'; he would soon transfer the command to Slocum. His later report puts his arrival at 3 p.m.; the 'an hour since' of the dispatch is carried as a conflict (arrival hour).

closeout.claim: Coulter's report of the First Brigade: the brigade, transferred to him about 5 p.m. on Jul 1 when the division was formed in the cemetery, retired through the town and was re-formed about 5 p.m.; later in the evening it moved toward the left, took position on the left of the Eleventh Corps and, having built breastworks of such materials as were at hand, remained there in support of the batteries until relieved by the Third Division, Second Corps, about noon the next day. 'About 7 o'clock in the evening' the brigade moved farther left to support the Third Corps under a considerable artillery fire, and 'about 10 p.m.' was placed on the Emmitsburg and Gettysburg road, from which it was relieved at daylight on the 3d: these two hours are Jul 2 (the Third Corps fought on Jul 2; the brigade is relieved on the 3d). The seed's 'moves left to support III Corps about 19:00' on Jul 1 is not supported. Other units of the division report the same evening works: the 107th Pennsylvania (threw up strong breastworks on the left of Cemetery Hill that night) and the 11th Pennsylvania (took position in rear of breastworks on the south side of the town), Baxter's brigade (temporary breastworks near the Emmitsburg road at about 5 p.m.).

closeout.claim: Johnson, marching from Scotland by the Cashtown road, did not arrive in time to take part in the fighting. Nicholls' brigade, in front, was at about 7 o'clock on the Cashtown road marching toward Gettysburg when Johnson ordered it east along the railroad about three-quarters of a mile from the town. Jones's brigade left camp at 7 a.m., reached the town 'late in the afternoon', passed the depot to the left of the town and formed line about dark; Richardson (42nd Virginia) puts the arrival 'about sunset'; Steuart's brigade came 'toward evening' and, marching through part of the town and along the York railroad, formed line to the northeast; Walker's brigade arrived on the evening and took position after nightfall on the southeast side of the town near the Hanover road, on Culp's farm. Johnson himself: 'late on the night of July 1' he formed line of battle in a ravine in an open field, Nicholls on the right next Jones, Steuart and Walker on the left, pickets well to the front, the troops sleeping on their arms. Lee: Johnson 'did not reach Gettysburg until a late hour'. All of these are carried as the arrival window; no single hour is picked.
remains_unsupported: A single hour for the head of the division at the town; Early's report p.470 says only 'at a late hour'.

closeout.claim: The National Park Service writes that the Mary Thompson House, built in the 1840s, served as Lee's headquarters and that on the morning of July 1, 1863 Lee rode just north of Gettysburg and established his headquarters in the farmstead residence of Mary Thompson. That differs from the seed's 'evening'; no Official Records passage names the Thompson house or gives Lee's place on the evening of Jul 1. The only place the sources name for Lee on the evening of Jul 1 is Early's account of a conference with Ewell and Rodes on the back porch of a small house north of the town near the Carlisle road. Longstreet (1896) reports to 'General Lee's head-quarters' at daylight on Jul 2 without naming a place. An illustration by Benson Lossing titled 'Confederate Headquarters' (a scene of September 1866, published in 1877) shows the repaired house (caption in the NPS landscape report); the same report says the house became famous for its association with Confederate headquarters following the Union retreat from Seminary Ridge on July 1, with the headquarters operations probably extending into the surrounding area, notably the Dustman orchard across the turnpike. The year of building (1833 Stone Sentinels; 1840s NPS), the 'Thaddeus Stevens building' reading of Wikipedia and the burning of Mary Thompson's fences for firewood have no passage in the local texts and stay unsupported. The seed itself calls Lee-in-the-cupola a rumour; no text read mentions it, and it is not shown.
remains_unsupported: The date and hour of establishment at the Thompson house; the building's year beyond the NPS 1840s (the seed's 1833 is a lead); the fence burning; any report naming the Thompson house on Jul 1.

closeout.claim: The National Park Service landscape report says: troops began to arrive on Cemetery Hill on July 1 when Howard posted a reserve of his Eleventh Corps; late in the day, as Union troops retreated, they reinforced the defensive lines around Cemetery Hill; lines of artillery were positioned near the summit along the northern and western borders of Evergreen Cemetery with caissons and horses among the grave plots; it was reported that General Howard ordered troops to lay the headstones flat on the ground to prevent their destruction; troops tore down wood and stone fences and rebuilt stone fences as breastworks. closeout.claim: On Jul 1 Greene's brigade was posted on the left with the division, about half a mile to the right of Sugar Loaf Mountain in front of the Taneytown road, with 'no incidents to note'; the division rested on its arms during the night. On Jul 2 Geary was relieved by the Third Corps and at 5 a.m. placed his division on the right of the centre of the line; Greene took position at about 6 a.m. on the crest of the hill and 'as soon as we were in position, we began to intrench ourselves and throw up breastworks'. Godard (60th New York): at or about 6 a.m. the regiment assumed position and threw up intrenchments by Greene's order, working until about 9 a.m. when they were completed; Ireland (137th): the breastworks were completed about noon; Hammerstein (78th): a breastwork of trees and dirt was soon thrown up; Stegman (102nd): the men were ordered to build breastworks of cord-wood and rock. Greene's report prints 'By 12 o'clock we had a good cover for the men': the OCR text reads '13 o'clock', and the printed number was read on the page image (printed page 856, PDF page 880 of the part-1 scan) as 12. The seed's 'construction began the night of Jul 1-2' (New York state agency page) is contradicted by Greene's and Geary's own accounts; the 'done about noon' (Gettysburg Daily) agrees with Ireland for one regiment.
remains_unsupported: The Gettysburg Daily '3 hours' reading (a lead, not read).

closeout.claim: Evening: Jacobs's record as relayed in 1885 (second-hand) has the sky covered with cirro-stratus at 9 p.m. and the thermometer at 74. Night: Everett says the full moon was veiled by thin clouds; Burling, at Emmitsburg, says the night was so very dark that his brigade could not march before about 4 a.m. after orders at 1.30 a.m.; the computed moon stood 30 degrees high from midnight to 2 a.m. (98.6-98.3 percent lit). Dawn: McAllister's brigade, within 2 miles of Gettysburg, recorded considerable fog at dawn. The seed's 'moon mostly hidden (darkest of the three nights)' and 'dew in low ground' have no passage; for the night of Jul 2-3 Geary reports 'dark night' with attacks in darkness, so the ranking is unsupported. Cloud over the moon is carried as scenarios (veiled by thin cloud against very dark).
remains_unsupported: Whether the moon was mostly hidden at Gettysburg; the ranking of the three nights; dew and fog on the night itself; Jacobs's original record.

closeout.claim: The corps' approach is as in T1-176: Geary advanced about 3 p.m., was sent by Hancock to the high ground near Round Top and by 5 p.m. was on the extreme left (so the seed's 'Cemetery Ridge' and its conflict with Geary at Culp's Hill on Jul 2 at 05:00 are resolved: Geary moved from the left to the right at 5 a.m. on Jul 2); Williams' division was called back and bivouacked near the Baltimore pike. The command: Hancock says he transferred it to Slocum between 5 and 6 o'clock; Howard writes that Hancock's written order reached him at 7 when Slocum had just arrived, and Meade and Howard have Slocum and Sickles at the cemetery about 7 p.m.; both are carried (T1-177). The seed's 'Hancock tells Slocum that Meade ordered him to take command' is not in Hancock's report or dispatch (he wrote that he would 'communicate with Slocum and transfer the command'); it is carried as unsupported in that wording.
remains_unsupported: The wording 'Hancock tells Slocum that Meade ordered him to take command' (not in Hancock's report).
